Then there is the delay from conversion to refund: a purchase that looks successful today may turn into a refund later. These two delays do not mean the same thing. A long wait before purchase may reflect hesitation, comparison, or careful intent. A later refund may reflect dissatisfaction, delivery trouble, price regret, or mismatch between expectation and product. The abstract says the two delays have opposite effects, so treating them as one waiting period hides the structure. Online systems make this harder because the data stream changes over time. User interests, products, promotions, and refund behavior can move, so a fixed model trained once may be learning yesterday's marketplace.
23.naive: A smart beginner would take the usual conversion-rate model and change the target label. Instead of asking whether a click became a purchase, it would ask whether a click became a purchase with no refund, then train one direct predictor for that final result. This sounds reasonable because net conversion rate is the desired business outcome. It fails because the final label is delayed and mixed. Early in the process, many clicks have not had enough time to convert, and many purchases have not had enough time to reveal refunds. A single final label also blurs two different behaviors: what makes someone buy and what makes someone return. The paper's evidence says modeling those stages separately works better than direct NetCVR modeling.
23.ap: The core idea is to respect the customer journey as a cascade instead of flattening it. The paper introduces CASCADE, an open large-scale dataset from the Taobao app for online continuous net conversion prediction. The dataset is meant to expose click, conversion, refund, and delay patterns that were previously hard to study openly. From that data, the authors report three guiding observations. Net conversion rate has clear temporal patterns, so the model must keep updating as new feedback arrives. Predicting conversion rate and refund rate as linked stages works better than trying to predict the final net result in one step. Delay time is not just a nuisance caused by slow feedback; it is itself useful evidence because it is correlated with both conversion and refund behavior. TESLA is the proposed method that uses these observations for continuous cascaded modeling and debiasing.
23.mech: The mechanism begins with a click on a recommended item. For that click, the system can observe user, item, time, and later feedback when it arrives. The first subproblem asks whether the click turns into a conversion. The second subproblem becomes relevant only after conversion: whether the purchase later becomes a refund. TESLA treats these as connected stages rather than independent labels scattered in a table. It models conversion rate and refund rate separately, then combines them to estimate net conversion rate, the chance that a clicked item is purchased and not refunded. Delay time enters as a feature, meaning the elapsed time between click and conversion or between conversion and refund is used as evidence about the stage. Online continuous modeling means the system is repeatedly refreshed as new clicks, purchases, and refunds arrive, instead of assuming one frozen training set describes the future. Debiasing is needed because feedback that has not arrived yet can make recent examples look falsely negative: a click may appear not to convert only because not enough time has passed, or a purchase may appear safely kept only because the refund window has not matured. The output is a score useful for recommender traffic allocation.
23.math: The main mathematical idea is probability over a chain of events. A probability is a disciplined estimate of how often an outcome should happen among many comparable cases, not a promise about one shopper. Here the outcome is compound: click leads to purchase, and purchase may lead to refund. Net conversion can be understood as the chance of passing the purchase gate and not passing the refund gate. Splitting the estimate into conversion rate and refund rate fits the world because the two gates are driven by different evidence and appear at different times. The second idea is time-aware learning. Delay is a measured quantity, not background noise. It changes how much trust to place in an observed label, because missing feedback may simply be immature feedback. The third idea is loss minimization, meaning the model defines what counts as a wrong prediction and changes its internal settings to reduce that wrongness as new cases arrive. The tradeoff is speed versus truth: the platform wants to rank products now, but the most honest signal, no refund, is only known later.
23.dots: This paper connects recommendation, e-commerce, probability, time-series modeling, and ranking. Like other recommender-system papers, it is about choosing a small set of items from a huge catalog under partial evidence. Its distinctive pressure is that the feedback used to judge the choice is delayed twice. That links it to broader probability work in the repo: many papers must act before complete evidence arrives, then update estimates as the evidence matures. It also belongs with advertising and e-commerce papers because the score controls traffic allocation, so a bad estimate spends user attention and marketplace exposure on the wrong products. Neighboring conversion and ranking work often tries to improve the meaning of a score by adding price, layout, multimodal product evidence, or fairness constraints. This paper repairs a more basic meaning problem: a conversion score should not count a regretted purchase as success.
23.ww: The method should improve on the naive approach because it matches the structure of the observed process. A direct NetCVR label asks the model to learn a final outcome that is both rare and late. That forces one predictor to infer purchase behavior, refund behavior, and missing-feedback timing all at once. Cascaded modeling gives each stage a cleaner job. The conversion part can focus on evidence that predicts buying after a click. The refund part can focus on evidence that predicts whether a completed purchase will be undone. Combining them then mirrors the real sequence: kept purchase requires both buying and not refunding. Delay time helps because lateness carries information and also warns against premature labels. Continuous updating helps because marketplace patterns are not stationary; user taste, product quality, promotions, and refund habits can change. The abstract's three CASCADE insights support the causal intuition that the model works by separating unlike signals before recombining them, rather than averaging them into one flat target.
23.po: The payoff is a more faithful score for recommender decisions. Instead of allocating traffic toward items that merely produce purchases, the platform can favor items more likely to be purchased and kept. The paper contributes CASCADE, described as the first large-scale open dataset for online continuous NetCVR prediction, which gives other researchers a shared way to study the problem. It also contributes TESLA, a continuous cascaded modeling and debiasing method grounded in the dataset's observed temporal patterns. The abstract reports that cascaded CVR and RFR modeling outperforms direct NetCVR modeling, so the practical gain is a better estimate of true recommendation effectiveness.
23.limits: The explanation depends on the abstract and repo data, so details beyond them remain unproven here. The abstract does not specify every feature used by TESLA, the exact debiasing formula, the deployment cost, or how performance varies across product categories. The approach assumes the Taobao-derived CASCADE patterns are useful for future online traffic and for other settings with similar click, purchase, and refund chains. It also assumes delay time is measured reliably and remains correlated with conversion and refund behavior. If refund policies, shipping conditions, promotions, or user groups change sharply, old delay patterns may mislead the model even with continuous updating.

24.bp: This paper serves the ordinary problem behind personalized federated learning: many clients want better models by learning from one another, but each client has its own data habits and cannot simply hand over raw data. A phone, hospital, browser, or local service may see examples that partly resemble everyone else's examples and partly reflect local needs. The shared part is valuable because no client has to learn from scratch. The personal part is also valuable because a single global model can smooth away exactly the distinctions that matter locally. Existing partial-sharing methods often split a neural network in a simple way: share the early feature extractor, meaning the part that turns raw inputs into internal descriptions, and keep the final classifier head local. pFedDKS asks whether that split is actually justified. Its answer is that personalization must reach deeper than the final decision layer, because the internal descriptions themselves can be mismatched between global sharing and local expectation.
24.wh: The hard part is that the system is trying to cooperate and specialize at the same time. If every client keeps a completely separate model, each one loses the benefit of patterns seen elsewhere. If every client shares too much, then local differences are averaged into a global view that may be clean for the group but wrong for a particular client. The abstract points to a specific tension inside the model. The feature extractor is not just a neutral preprocessor. It decides what differences in the raw input are kept and what differences are compressed away before classification happens. Earlier methods often assumed this whole extractor could be shared while only the classifier head stayed personal. The paper argues that this assumption breaks because the fused global feature representations do not match the expected local feature representations. In plain terms, the common internal language learned from many clients can describe examples in a way that a local client would not choose for itself.
24.naive: A smart beginner would divide the model at the obvious boundary. Let everyone share the feature extractor, since basic patterns may seem reusable across clients, and let each client customize only the classifier head, since labels and final decisions may differ locally. This is attractive because it is easy to manage: one shared body, many local heads. The failure is that the body is already making personal choices before the head sees anything. If the shared extractor groups examples using global averages, the local head receives descriptions that may be tilted away from the client's own data. The client can adjust the final decision rule, but it cannot fully repair a representation that has already hidden or distorted useful local structure.
24.ap: The core idea is to detach shared knowledge from local knowledge earlier in the network instead of pretending that the entire feature extractor is safe to share. pFedDKS uses the theory of neural collapse, which studies how trained classifiers tend to arrange examples and class representatives in their internal descriptions, to inspect what full feature sharing does. The paper reports a substantial inconsistency between fused global feature representations and expected local feature representations. From that observation, it proposes partial sharing inside the feature extractor: keep some layers shared so clients can still borrow common structure, but preserve some customized extractor layers so local representation can form. The method then provides detached feature prototypes. A prototype is a representative internal description, like a learned reference point for a class or pattern. Detaching prototypes gives the system separate handles for global and local knowledge rather than forcing both through one fused description.
24.mech: The mechanism starts with several clients, each holding its own data and participating in a federated training process. Each client has a neural network with a feature extractor and a classifier head. The feature extractor turns raw examples into internal descriptions; the classifier head uses those descriptions to choose labels. A standard partial-sharing design would aggregate the extractor across clients and leave the classifier head customized. pFedDKS changes that division. First, it treats the extractor as something with layers that can play different roles, not as one indivisible shared block. Some extractor layers carry global knowledge, meaning patterns that many clients can reuse. Other extractor layers remain customized, meaning they are allowed to shape descriptions around the client's own data. Second, the method uses detached feature prototypes to separate the two kinds of knowledge. The abstract does not give implementation details, but the supported picture is that these prototypes act as reference descriptions for what global and local features should look like. During training, clients can compare or align their internal descriptions with the appropriate prototypes without collapsing all representation into one global form. What comes out is still a personalized federated model, but its personalization is not limited to the last classifier head. It also changes how examples are represented before final decisions are made.
24.math: The main mathematical idea is representation geometry, explained here as the shape made by examples after a model has turned raw inputs into internal descriptions. If two examples are treated as similar, their descriptions sit close together; if they are treated as different, they sit apart. The feature extractor is the part that creates this geometry. Neural collapse gives the paper a way to reason about a trained classifier's late-stage geometry: examples from the same class and their class reference directions tend to settle into a highly organized arrangement. The abstract says pFedDKS uses this theory to show that fully sharing the extractor is not appropriate. The mathematical pressure is a mismatch between two geometries. One geometry is fused from global sharing across clients. The other is the local geometry a client would expect from its own data. Prototypes are the second key object. A prototype is a representative point or direction in this internal geometry, a compact stand-in for a class or learned pattern. Detached prototypes let global and local structure be represented separately. The tradeoff is shared evidence versus local detail. Sharing more reduces duplication and lets clients learn from others, but it can move internal descriptions toward an average that harms personalization.
24.dots: This paper belongs to the privacy and federated-security family because it asks what useful signal may cross a boundary without moving each client's raw data. It connects most directly to the personalization branch of that family, alongside papers in the repo such as FedRMamba, MF3, FedCND, Thorki, PAECL, prototype-aligned soft prompts, and verifiable federated recommendation, where clients are not treated as identical copies. It also connects to the broader conference idea of selective focus: systems must decide which parts of a model, history, graph neighborhood, document, or signal deserve shared influence and which should remain local or downweighted. Mathematically, it sits near learning from examples and similarity. It learns reusable patterns from many clients, but the paper's key warning is that similarity itself can be client-specific. Two examples that are close under a global representation may not be close in the way a local client needs for its own decisions.
24.ww: The method should work better than the naive split because it moves personalization to the place where many important choices are first made. A classifier head can only act on the descriptions it receives. If those descriptions are already formed by a fully shared extractor, then local customization is like relabeling a map whose roads were drawn for a different city. pFedDKS changes the map-making step. By preserving partially customized extractor layers, each client can keep internal distinctions that matter for its own data. By keeping some shared layers, the client still benefits from patterns learned across other clients. Detached feature prototypes help because they make the separation explicit. Instead of mixing global and local reference points into one fused target, the model can carry common reference descriptions and personal reference descriptions with different roles. The neural-collapse argument matters because it gives a principled reason to expect representation mismatch, not just an empirical complaint. If class descriptions settle into different arrangements globally and locally, then forcing one arrangement onto all clients naturally weakens personalization.
24.po: The payoff is a more careful form of personalized federated learning. The paper claims both theoretical and empirical evidence that the feature extractor should be partially shared rather than fully shared, and it turns that finding into pFedDKS. In practical terms, the capability bought is collaboration without forcing every client into the same internal description of the world. The abstract says experiments across various datasets and models show pFedDKS outperforming state-of-the-art methods. The important result is not just a higher score; it is evidence that personalization sometimes requires customized representation layers, not only customized final decision heads.
24.limits: The abstract supports the representation-mismatch claim, but it does not provide the full proof, datasets, model families, or conditions under which the split is best. The method assumes clients share enough structure that some global knowledge is useful, while differing enough that local extractor customization matters. If clients are nearly identical, the extra separation may add little. If clients are extremely different, even shared layers or prototypes may transfer weakly. The explanation also depends on neural-collapse theory being an appropriate lens for the studied networks and training settings. The abstract reports broad experiments, but it does not prove the same behavior for every architecture, client population, label pattern, or privacy threat.

25.bp: A recommender system does more than choose products, posts, or videos. It also has to tell a person why those choices make sense. That explanation can shape trust: a user may accept a recommendation because the system says it noticed recent browsing, repeated purchases, or a shift in taste. RobustExplain studies the reliability of that explanation layer when the history fed to a large language model is messy. The real-world object is a user behavior history on a web platform, not a clean profile. It can contain accidental clicks, missing entries, events in the wrong order, and preferences that change over time. The paper asks whether an explanation agent still gives a stable account of the recommendation when that history is perturbed in realistic ways. Its goal is evaluation, not a new recommender. It builds a way to measure whether natural-language explanations remain meaningfully consistent under noise.
25.wh: The hard part is that an explanation can sound fluent while being fragile. A language model may produce a polished sentence that mentions the user liked outdoor gear, budget phones, or mystery novels, but the paper's concern is whether the same basic reason survives when the input history is slightly damaged. Recommendation histories are especially troublesome because they mix true preference with accidents. A click may happen by mistake, an item may be missing from a log, and yesterday's interest may not match today's intent. If the model treats every event as equally meaningful, a small noisy change can redirect the story. If it ignores too much, it may miss genuine preference changes. Previous work, according to the abstract, has mostly judged fluency and relevance under fixed inputs. That leaves a gap: a fixed-input explanation can look good while failing the more practical test of staying trustworthy when ordinary web data is imperfect.
25.naive: A smart beginner would give the user history to a strong language model, ask for a concise explanation, and then judge whether the result reads well and mentions relevant items. That is a sensible first check because users experience explanations as language. But it fails because it tests the explanation only in a clean, frozen situation. The same model might say one thing when an accidental click is present and a different thing when that click is removed. It might change length, structure, key words, or the central meaning even though the user's real preference has not changed. Fluency therefore becomes a weak safety signal: the words can be smooth while the reasoning is unstable.
25.ap: RobustExplain's central move is to turn explanation reliability into a controlled stress test. Instead of asking only whether one explanation sounds relevant, it deliberately changes the user behavior history in five realistic ways and watches how the generated explanation changes. The perturbations are tested at multiple severity levels, so the evaluator can ask not just whether the explanation breaks, but how quickly it breaks as noise grows. The output is judged along several dimensions: whether the main meaning is preserved, whether important words remain, whether the structure of the explanation stays similar, and whether the length swings unexpectedly. This makes robustness a task-level measurement. The paper is careful about scope: it aims to provide a principled evaluation framework and initial baselines across four representative large language models, not a complete leaderboard of all possible models.
25.mech: The mechanism begins with a recommendation setting where a language model receives a user's behavior history and produces a natural-language explanation. RobustExplain then creates altered versions of that history. The abstract names the kinds of real noise it wants to represent: accidental clicks, temporal inconsistencies, missing values, and evolving preferences; it also says the framework has five realistic perturbations, though the provided text does not list all five in detail. Each perturbation is applied at multiple severity levels, which means the test can compare small disturbances with stronger ones instead of treating noise as a single condition. For every original or altered history, the explanation agent generates text. The evaluation then compares the resulting explanations across four views. Semantic consistency asks whether the explanation still says the same basic thing. Keyword consistency asks whether important terms survive. Structural consistency asks whether the organization of the explanation remains comparable. Length consistency asks whether the model suddenly becomes much shorter or longer. These measurements are combined into a multi-dimensional robustness metric. The paper runs this procedure on four representative language models ranging from 7 billion to 70 billion parameters, then reports that current models have only moderate stability, with larger models reaching up to 8 percent higher stability.
25.math: The main mathematical idea is controlled comparison under disturbance. Start with one object, a user history, and one produced object, an explanation. Then change the input in a known way and measure how much the output changes. This is the everyday idea behind robustness: if the real preference signal is mostly the same, a trustworthy explanation should not swing wildly because one click was accidental or one value is missing. The perturbation levels create a scale of damage, like turning a dial from mild noise to stronger noise. The four consistency measurements turn different kinds of sameness into scores. Semantic consistency compares meaning, not just surface wording. Keyword consistency counts whether salient terms are retained. Structural consistency compares the shape of the explanation, such as whether the same kinds of reasons are organized similarly. Length consistency treats unexplained expansion or collapse as evidence of instability. The underlying tradeoff is sensitivity versus steadiness. An explanation agent should be sensitive enough to reflect real preference changes, but steady enough to ignore harmless log noise. The math fits because the paper is not trying to prove the one true explanation; it is measuring whether explanations remain close when inputs are changed in realistic, controlled ways.
25.dots: This paper belongs to the recommender-systems family because it treats recommendation as more than ranking a small set from a large pile. The system must also justify the choice in a way users can trust. It connects to the explainability and interpretability family in the repo, where the shared pressure is that a correct-looking output is not enough unless the evidence behind it can be inspected. RobustExplain adds a sharper test: the explanation must remain stable when the evidence is noisy. It also sits near the LLM agents and tool-use family because the language model is acting as an explanation agent over an external record rather than merely answering from memory. The mathematical neighbors are similarity and ranking. Similarity appears because explanations under perturbed histories must be compared for closeness in meaning, words, structure, and length. Ranking appears because the whole setting begins with a recommender deciding what deserves attention.
25.ww: The approach works better than the naive check because it changes the question from, Does this one explanation look good, to, Does this explanation behave sensibly under realistic input damage. A single clean example cannot reveal whether a model is following stable preference evidence or chasing whichever detail appears most recent or most vivid in the log. Perturbations expose that difference. If an accidental click causes the explanation to focus on a new preference, semantic consistency drops. If missing data makes the model omit key item words, keyword consistency drops. If the model changes from a reasoned account to a different shape of response, structural consistency drops. If the response length moves sharply without a clear reason, length consistency catches another kind of instability. Multiple severity levels make the evaluation more informative because a model that survives mild noise but fails heavy noise is different from one that fails immediately. Comparing 7B to 70B models also tests whether model size alone buys stability; the abstract says it helps only modestly.
25.po: The payoff is a practical measuring stick for a failure mode that recommendation systems can otherwise hide. RobustExplain gives researchers a way to test explanation agents under noisy user histories, using five perturbation types, several noise strengths, and four consistency dimensions. The reported result is not that current systems are solved, but the opposite: four representative large language models show only moderate robustness, and larger models improve stability by up to 8 percent. That matters because it turns user trust from a vague concern into something that can be stressed, compared, and improved.
25.limits: The abstract supports an evaluation contribution, not a guarantee that any explanation is faithful to the recommender's true internal decision. Consistency is also not the same as correctness: a model could give the same wrong explanation after every perturbation. The perturbations must resemble real platform noise for the metric to predict deployed behavior. The model set is representative but limited to four language models from 7B to 70B parameters, and the paper explicitly avoids claiming a comprehensive leaderboard. The abstract also does not prove how the metric should be weighted for different users, platforms, cultures, or trust-sensitive domains.

26.bp: A large language model used for search or dialogue has to answer many different requests quickly. One way to make such a model large without running every part on every request is to split it into many expert parts and let a router choose a small team for the current input. The ordinary problem is a dispatch problem: for this question, which workers should be called, and how can the system avoid wasting time making the same dispatch decision again and again? The paper studies Mixture-of-Experts models, where the model has many expert networks but activates only some of them. The abstract says current routing is often stateless, meaning the router does not keep a useful memory of which expert teams worked for earlier, similar inputs. RMS-MoE treats routing less like a one-time guess and more like a reusable memory problem for web-scale question answering and dialogue.
26.wh: The hard part is that routing must be both cheap and correct. If the router spends too much computation deciding which experts should handle a request, the system loses the speed advantage that expert models were supposed to provide. If it routes too casually, the wrong experts may be activated, hurting accuracy or making related inputs behave differently. Web-scale search and dialogue make this worse because many inputs are not identical, but they are related in meaning. A user may ask the same need with different wording, or a conversation may circle back to a similar topic. A stateless router treats each case as fresh, so it repeatedly re-explores expert assignments. That creates computational redundancy and unstable behavior. The tension is memory versus adaptation: reuse past routing when the new input resembles old ones, but still notice when the current input needs a different expert team.
26.naive: A smart beginner might keep the usual live router and ask it to choose experts from scratch for every input. That is simple because the model only needs the current request, not a separate memory system. The failure is repetition. If many semantically related inputs arrive, the router keeps rediscovering similar expert teams, paying the same decision cost again. Another beginner fix would be a plain cache: if the exact same input appears, reuse the old experts. That also fails because web and dialogue inputs rarely repeat word for word. The useful sameness is meaning-level sameness, not exact text identity. The paper's problem begins in that gap between exact repetition and related requests.
26.ap: The core idea is to give the router a memory of expert teamwork. RMS-MoE adds a Co-Activation Memory, which stores effective expert teams that have worked together for earlier inputs. When a new input arrives, the system retrieves routing memories for semantically related inputs, meaning inputs judged similar in what they are asking about rather than identical in wording. Those retrieved memories act as priors: informed starting beliefs about which experts are likely to be useful. The model does not blindly copy them. It also computes live routing predictions for the current input, then uses a learnable input-dependent gate to fuse the two sources. In plain terms, the gate decides how much to trust remembered expert teams and how much to trust the fresh routing signal. The result is expert coordination that can be consistent across related inputs while still responding to the current request.
26.mech: The mechanism starts with an input from a web question-answering or dialogue task. First, the model forms the information needed for routing: what kind of request this appears to be and which experts might help. In an ordinary expert model, the live router would use only this current signal to select experts. RMS-MoE adds a second path. It queries the Co-Activation Memory for past cases that are semantically related to the current input. The memory returns effective expert teams that were previously co-activated, so the system sees not just isolated expert choices but combinations that have worked together. Those retrieved teams become a prior routing suggestion. In parallel, the live router produces its own current prediction. The learnable gate then combines the retrieved prior and the live prediction. Because the gate depends on the input, it can give more weight to memory when the current input looks like familiar territory and more weight to live routing when the input seems less covered by past cases. The fused routing decision selects the expert team to activate. The model then runs only those chosen experts, coordinates their outputs inside the larger language model, and produces the answer or dialogue continuation. The output of the mechanism is therefore not only text; it is also a more stable routing pattern for related future requests.
26.math: Several mathematical ideas are doing work here. The first is similarity: the system must decide when two inputs are close enough in meaning that a past expert team is useful for the new one. Similarity is a compression of many differences into a usable comparison, so it gains speed and reuse while risking mistakes when two inputs sound related but need different expertise. The second idea is retrieval: instead of recomputing everything, look up nearby past cases and bring back the evidence most likely to help. The third is probability-like weighting through a prior. A retrieved expert team is not a command; it is a starting belief shaped by past success. The live router supplies current evidence, and the gate mixes old belief with new evidence. That is a balancing problem: memory saves computation and encourages consistency, while fresh routing protects against stale or misleading memories. The fourth idea is optimization, meaning the system learns settings that reduce routing error, latency, or instability according to training feedback. The gate is learnable because fixed hand rules would not know when memory should dominate and when the current input should override it. The tradeoff is speed and stability versus the risk of overusing remembered patterns.
26.dots: This paper sits where several recurring conference ideas meet. It is about language models, but the deeper problem is retrieval: choose a small useful set from a large store, here expert teams rather than documents. It also connects to recommendation and ranking, because the router ranks experts by expected usefulness under limited compute. It connects to systems work because the scarce resource is latency: the abstract reports a 26% latency reduction, so saving routing effort matters in deployed search and dialogue. It connects to probability and learning because the retrieved memory is only partial evidence, not proof, and the gate must learn how strongly to use it. Neighboring retrieval-augmented language-model papers often retrieve facts or documents to ground answers; this one retrieves coordination patterns inside the model itself. The common shape is reuse: past structure can make the next decision cheaper and steadier if the system can tell when the past is relevant.
26.ww: The mechanism should work because similar requests often need similar internal labor. If two search questions or dialogue turns ask about related material, the same group of expert networks may contain the useful behavior for both. A stateless router ignores that repetition, so it spends computation rediscovering a team and may choose a slightly different team for nearly the same need. RMS-MoE changes the starting point. Retrieved co-activation memories give the router a well-informed suggestion before it has to decide from scratch. That reduces repeated search through expert assignments. The live router and the gate matter because memory alone would be too rigid. If the retrieved teams agree with the current signal, the system can route confidently and consistently. If they differ, the learned gate can lean toward the fresh evidence. This explains the abstract's three reported gains together: lower latency comes from less repeated routing effort, better accuracy can come from reusing effective teams, and better routing stability comes from giving related inputs a shared routing history.
26.po: The payoff is a more practical expert-based language model for web-scale use. According to the abstract, RMS-MoE reduces latency by 26%, gains 2.7 accuracy points, and improves routing stability by 3.3% on question-answering and dialogue tasks. Those numbers matter because deployed search and conversational systems need more than strong answers in isolation. They need fast responses, predictable behavior for related requests, and efficient use of computation. The paper's contribution is to show that architectural memory can be useful inside the routing machinery itself, not only as external knowledge retrieved for final answer generation.
26.limits: The claims depend on the memory retrieving genuinely related inputs and on past expert teams remaining useful for new cases. If the similarity search confuses surface resemblance with real task resemblance, the memory may push the router toward the wrong experts. If user needs, topics, or model behavior change over time, stored co-activations may become stale. The abstract reports experiments on web-scale question answering and dialogue, but it does not prove the same gains for every language-model task or every expert architecture. It also does not specify, in the abstract, the cost of storing, updating, and searching the Co-Activation Memory, which must be counted in a real deployment.

27.bp: A shopping recommender is not only deciding which product page to show. It is also quietly deciding which purchasable version of that product the user is likely to choose. One listing can hide many stock keeping units: different package sizes, colors, bundles, qualities, or other variants, and those variants can sit at different prices. The paper's real-world problem is that large e-commerce systems often predict conversion at the item level, while the actual purchase happens at this finer SKU level. That gap matters because price is part of user intent. A user who clicks a product after seeing one price may buy a different priced variant, or may only be interested if the affordable version is the one being shown. PSKU4Rec serves a marketplace decision loop: estimate whether a user will buy, refine the predicted conversion chance using a personalized expected transaction price, and even choose a main product image that better matches the user's likely price-level preference.
27.wh: The hard part is a granularity mismatch. Item-level prediction is cheap enough for industrial recommendation, but it treats all variants inside one product as if they carried the same buying signal. SKU-level prediction is closer to the actual purchase, but the abstract says direct SKU modeling is impractical because the data becomes extremely sparse and inference costs become prohibitive. Sparsity means many specific user-SKU pairs have few or no past observations, so the model cannot reliably learn whether that exact variant attracts that exact kind of user. Cost matters because a production recommender may need to score huge numbers of candidates quickly. Price adds a second failure mode: the exposure price shown when the item is recommended can differ from the transaction price at purchase time. If the model learns from static exposure prices while users act on actual variant prices, the score can become price-inconsistent, rewarding the wrong item-price combination.
27.naive: A smart beginner would try one of two direct fixes. The first is to keep the current item-level model and add price as another feature, hoping the model learns that cheaper or premium variants convert differently. That still leaves many SKU-level signals mixed together inside one item score. The second is to model every SKU separately, which seems conceptually clean because purchases happen at SKU level. The abstract explains why this breaks in deployment: individual SKUs are too numerous and too thinly observed, so many of them lack enough examples, and scoring them all would be too expensive. The simple item view loses intent; the simple SKU view preserves detail but becomes too sparse and slow.
27.ap: The central move is to choose a middle unit: the Price SKU, or PSKU. Instead of treating the whole item as one object, and instead of treating every exact SKU as its own object, the method groups SKUs by price. This keeps a price-level signal, which is critical for conversion, while reducing the number of separate units the model must learn. The abstract reports that this aggregation reduces sparsity by six times. PSKU4Rec then gives the recommender two connected abilities. First, a PSKU-aware prediction network models context among price groups within the same item and captures each user's PSKU preferences. Second, an application module uses those learned preferences to estimate a personalized transaction price for conversion-rate refinement and to choose a personalized main image. The paper is therefore not only predicting purchase probability; it is repairing the unit of prediction so the score matches how buying actually happens.
27.mech: The mechanism starts with ordinary e-commerce logs from Taobao App: users see item exposures at shown prices, interact with products, and sometimes complete transactions at actual SKU prices. The input item is decomposed into price-based groups of SKUs. This creates PSKU units inside the item, coarse enough to have more observations than individual SKUs but fine enough to preserve meaningful price differences. The prediction network then considers two kinds of information. One is intra-item PSKU context: how the price groups inside the same product relate to one another, such as budget and premium versions competing under the same item identity. The other is user PSKU preference: whether this user appears more likely to convert at certain price levels within items. These signals produce a conversion estimate that is aware of price-level intent rather than only item identity. The application module then turns that estimate into serving-time actions. It generates a personalized estimated transaction price, using the user's likely PSKU preference to refine the predicted conversion rate. It also enables personalized main-image display, which means the visual representation of the item can be aligned with the price-grouped variant the user is most likely to buy. The output is a recommendation score and presentation choice that better match the eventual transaction unit.
27.math: The main mathematical idea is probability under the right unit of counting. Conversion rate is a chance estimate: among comparable recommendation moments, how often does exposure lead to purchase? If comparable cases are defined only by item, the estimate averages over several hidden price choices. If comparable cases are defined by exact SKU, there may be too few repeated cases to trust. PSKU aggregation changes the sample groups so the chance estimate is neither too blurry nor too thin. A second idea is ranking, because the predicted conversion rate helps decide which products should rise near the top of a huge catalog where only a few can be shown. The score is useful only if it orders item-price possibilities in a way that matches real buying intent. A third idea is representation learning, meaning the system learns compact descriptions of users, items, and price groups from examples rather than relying on a hand-written rule like lower price always wins. The tradeoff is compression versus detail. Grouping SKUs by price discards some variant-specific information, but it keeps the detail the abstract identifies as critical while making the evidence dense enough and the serving computation cheap enough for large-scale recommendation.
27.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of recommender systems, e-commerce, ranking, probability, and similarity. The repo's recommender family frames the shared problem as choosing a small useful set from a huge changing pile under partial evidence. Here, the hidden difficulty is that the candidate is not just an item; it is an item at a likely transaction price. The advertising and e-commerce family notes the same marketplace pressure: a simple score is often too flat for the decision it controls, and this paper is one of the clearest examples because item-level conversion hides price-level behavior. It also connects to broader ranking work, where the score is only a handle for ordering candidates under scarce attention. It connects to probability work because the model estimates a purchase chance before the purchase is known, from repeated but biased marketplace logs. It connects to similarity and learning because users with related price preferences and PSKU contexts supply evidence for one another.
27.ww: The method should work better than the naive item-level model because it lines up the model's categories with the buyer's actual choice. If users are deciding among price-bearing variants, then averaging all variants into one item score hides a real cause of different purchase behavior. PSKU groups expose that cause without exploding the problem into every exact SKU. The six-times sparsity reduction reported in the abstract matters because probability estimates improve when each group has enough repeated cases to reveal a stable pattern. The PSKU-aware prediction network can learn, for example, that the same user may be willing to buy a lower-priced version of one item but not a premium version, or that certain price groups inside an item explain why exposure and transaction prices disagree. The application module then uses the learned price preference at serving time, so the conversion score is refined toward an estimated transaction price rather than frozen at the exposure price. Personalized image display helps for the same reason: the shown product representation can point toward the variant the user is more likely to consider.
27.po: The payoff is a recommender score that better reflects how purchases actually occur in an e-commerce catalog. PSKU4Rec keeps critical price signals, reduces SKU-level sparsity by six times, refines predicted conversion rate with personalized estimated transaction prices, and supports personalized main-image display. The abstract reports offline improvements on Taobao App data in both conversion-rate prediction accuracy and price consistency. It also says online A/B testing validates the approach. In practical terms, the system can allocate recommendation slots with less confusion between shown item price and eventual transaction price, which should make ranking and product presentation more faithful to user intent.
27.limits: The abstract does not specify the exact grouping rule for prices, the features used by the prediction network, the size of the Taobao dataset, or how gains vary across categories. The approach assumes price-grouped SKUs preserve the important variant signal; if non-price attributes such as size, color, brand bundle, or availability drive conversion more than price, PSKU grouping may still blur intent. It also assumes historical exposure and transaction logs are reliable guides to future behavior. Promotions, seller changes, inventory shifts, or altered display policies could change the relationship between price groups and conversion. Online A/B validation supports deployment value, but the abstract does not prove generality across other platforms.

28.bp: A data market is supposed to let one party sell useful records and another party train a model from them without exposing the private details inside those records. The hard object is not just the dataset. It is the whole trade: owners want payment and privacy, buyers want data that still teaches a model, and the market platform must not become an all-seeing middleman. Xemis serves this setting. It asks how a market can add carefully measured random blur to traded data so individual records are protected, while the buyer still receives enough signal for model training. The paper focuses on differential privacy, which means each person's record should have only a limited visible effect on the released result. But in a trade, the question immediately becomes practical: who is trusted to create exactly the right blur, deliver the data fairly, and resist market nodes that may cheat?
28.wh: The central tension is that privacy noise must be both hidden and exact. If the noise is too small, sensitive records may leak. If it is too large, the bought data becomes less useful and the buyer may pay for damaged goods. If one trusted third party creates the noise, raw data or perturbed data can pass through a place that everyone must trust. If the data owner creates the noise alone, the buyer may suspect the owner added the wrong amount or shaped the data unfairly. The abstract says existing differential-privacy approaches struggle to inject precisely calibrated noise in a trustworthy way without revealing raw data to a third party. Malicious outside attackers and a corrupted data market make this worse, because the system cannot assume every participant follows the protocol. Fairness is therefore tied to privacy: payment, value assessment, and delivery must remain credible while nobody sees what they should not see.
28.naive: A smart beginner would build a normal data platform and add a privacy step before delivery. The seller uploads data, the market adds Gaussian noise, the buyer receives the blurred version, and payment follows. That fails because the market sees too much and becomes the party everyone must trust. A second beginner would let the seller add the noise before upload. That protects raw data from the market, but now the buyer and market cannot easily know whether the noise was calibrated to the agreed privacy level or whether delivery was fair. A third beginner might split trust among many market nodes without a careful protocol. That helps only if cheating nodes cannot bias the noise, block delivery, or distort value assessment.
28.ap: Xemis changes the trade from a single trusted noise maker into a distributed procedure. Its main building block is b-DNS, a batched distributed noise sharing protocol built with multi-party computation. In plain terms, the market nodes jointly create pieces of Gaussian random noise, but no one node owns the whole noise value and no one needs to see the raw data. The paper uses threshold secret shares, meaning the useful value exists only when enough pieces are combined, while too few pieces reveal nothing useful by themselves. Xemis then applies those shared noise pieces to blinded data shares under a controllable privacy level. The abstract also adds two market-side mechanisms: a game-theoretic mechanism to shape incentives and a distributed demo-dataset sampling mechanism with Byzantine fault tolerant consensus to support fair value assessment and payment-data delivery. The core move is to make privacy, fairness, and delivery collective checks rather than promises from one marketplace.
28.mech: The mechanism begins with a data owner, a buyer, and a decentralized market made of many nodes. The owner's raw data is not handed to one market operator. Instead, the data is blinded and represented through shares, so each node handles only a protected piece. Separately, b-DNS makes the noise needed for differential privacy. It generates Gaussian samples as threshold secret shares: each participant receives a piece, and the pieces together behave like the desired random blur. Because this is batched, many random bits and samples are produced together rather than one expensive cryptographic operation at a time. The batched bits expansion mechanism stretches the work efficiently, which the abstract connects to much lower computation and communication cost than older protocols. Next, the market perturbs the blinded data shares with the shared noise at the chosen privacy level. The market should not see either the original raw data or the final perturbed data while this happens. To handle cheating, the protocol is Byzantine robust, meaning it is designed to keep working when some nodes act maliciously instead of merely failing silently. For value and payment, Xemis samples distributed demo datasets and uses Byzantine fault tolerant consensus so nodes can agree on assessment and delivery. The output is data whose privacy blur is controlled, whose raw contents remain hidden from the market, and whose trade process supports fair payment and delivery.
28.math: The first mathematical idea is differential privacy: hide any single record by adding random noise so that the released data would look almost the same whether that record were present or absent. The privacy budget is the dial that says how much visible influence one record is allowed to have. Xemis uses Gaussian noise, ordinary bell-shaped random variation, because many privacy methods can translate a desired protection level into a needed amount of such noise. The second idea is secret sharing. A value is broken into pieces so that one piece is useless alone, while enough pieces reconstruct or act like the value collectively. Here the value is not only data but also the noise that must be trusted. The third idea is multi-party computation, where several parties jointly compute a result while keeping their private pieces hidden. The fourth idea is Byzantine robustness: the calculation must tolerate participants that send bad messages, not just participants that crash. Finally, game-theoretic design treats market nodes as strategic actors with incentives. The tradeoff is privacy versus utility, because more noise protects records but harms training; trust versus cost, because stronger distributed checks require communication; and fairness versus adversarial freedom, because payment and delivery rules must limit profitable cheating.
28.dots: Xemis belongs to the privacy, federated, and security family because it asks what useful signal may cross a boundary without exposing the private object behind it. It sits beside federated-learning papers that keep raw data on devices, but its surface setting is a market rather than a training collaboration. The same deeper pressure appears: cooperation is valuable, yet the act of cooperation creates leakage and attack surfaces. It also connects to matching and market papers, because data owners, buyers, and market nodes need an exchange that makes value and payment line up. The trust family connection is direct as well: like zero-knowledge and provenance work, Xemis replaces faith in a central actor with a procedure that can be checked under limited visibility. Mathematically, it touches probability through calibrated random noise, optimization and incentives through game-theoretic market design, and distributed systems through consensus under malicious nodes.
28.ww: The approach should improve over the naive trusted-market design because it removes the single place where privacy and fairness can collapse together. If one marketplace node created the whole noisy dataset, corrupting or observing that node could expose raw data, alter the noise, or bias delivery. By splitting both data handling and noise generation into shares, Xemis makes each participant's view incomplete. That means an attacker has less direct material to steal, and a corrupted node has less ability to secretly choose the final privacy blur. Precise Gaussian noise matters because differential privacy is not just add some randomness; it depends on adding the right amount for the promised privacy budget. The b-DNS protocol targets exactly that calibration while keeping the process distributed. Batching helps because cryptographic safety is often too expensive if every random bit is produced separately. The reported speed and bandwidth gains matter only because they make the stronger trust structure plausible for a real market. Consensus and demo-dataset sampling then address the business side: participants need agreement about value, payment, and delivery, not only hidden computation.
28.po: The payoff is a data trading design where useful training data can be sold without asking the market platform to see raw or perturbed data. The abstract reports controllable privacy, strong fairness, Web3 compatibility, and tolerance of malicious market nodes. It also reports that b-DNS is at least 12.7 times faster and uses at least 43.6 times less bandwidth than two earlier protocols, and that Xemis is at least 3.3 times faster than ZLM+24 with a 64-node market. For utility, the abstract evaluates noise-perturbed data on CIFAR-10 image classification and reports 83 percent accuracy when noise with privacy budget 1 is added to 63 percent of the training data.
28.limits: The claims depend on the protocol assumptions holding: enough market nodes must follow the rules, the threshold for secret shares must be chosen correctly, and the modeled Byzantine behavior must cover the important attacks. The abstract does not prove that every real data market has honest participation, reliable identity, or incentives strong enough to stop collusion. The utility evidence is from CIFAR-10 image classification, so it does not establish the same usefulness for medical records, transactions, text, or sparse business data. The privacy guarantee also depends on the chosen budget and noise calibration. Stronger privacy may lower utility, and the abstract does not show all tradeoffs across data types, buyer goals, or market sizes.

29.bp: A retrieval-augmented answer system has two parts that must cooperate. First it searches a document collection for passages related to a question. Then a large language model reads those passages and writes an answer. The paper starts from a practical weakness in that arrangement: the system often behaves as if every retrieved passage is equally worth listening to. In real use, that is false. One document may directly answer the question, another may be only loosely related, and another may be present because the search step made a noisy match. OpenDecoder serves the ordinary need of making generated answers depend more on useful outside evidence and less on weak context. The paper's central concern is not merely finding documents; it is deciding how much the answer-writing stage should trust each retrieved piece. That matters whenever a user expects a grounded answer rather than a fluent answer built from uneven support.
29.wh: The hard part is that relevance is not a simple yes-or-no property. A document can share words with the question but fail to contain the needed fact. It can be ranked highly by the retrieval system yet still be less useful than a lower-ranked document. It can help one question while distracting from another question asked over the same collection. The abstract says RAG work often assumes that retrieved information is relevant, but retrieved information actually has varying degrees of relevance and usefulness. That creates a tension inside answer generation: the language model must use outside material, but using all of it with equal force can pull the answer toward noise. The model's internal information processing may not automatically know which retrieved pieces deserve more influence. The difficulty is therefore a trust-weighting problem under imperfect search, where the answer stage must read evidence without being dominated by the weakest evidence.
29.naive: A smart beginner would retrieve the top few documents, paste them all into the model's input, and ask the model to answer from that context. This is sensible because the documents were selected by a retrieval system, so they should be more useful than the model guessing from memory. The failure is that top retrieved does not mean equally trustworthy. If the first passage is only partly related, if several passages repeat background but not the answer, or if the collection has noisy matches, the model may blend them into a confident but poorly grounded response. Adding more retrieved text can even worsen the problem by increasing distraction. The missing step is an explicit estimate of document quality at the moment the answer is being written.
29.ap: OpenDecoder's core move is to open the answer-writing stage to quality signals about the retrieved documents. Instead of treating retrieved passages as an undifferentiated block of context, it feeds the generation process explicit indicator features that describe how useful each retrieved item appears to be. The abstract names three such signals: a relevance score, a ranking score, and a QPP score, where query performance prediction estimates how well the retrieval step is likely to have served this particular question. In plain terms, the model is not only given the evidence; it is also given labels about how much confidence the retrieval system has in that evidence. The method therefore shifts RAG from read whatever was fetched to read while knowing which witnesses look stronger. The goal is better behavior when the retrieved context contains different levels of noise.
29.mech: The mechanism can be read as a pipeline with an extra information channel. The input is a user question and a document collection. A retriever searches the collection and returns candidate documents or passages. In a standard RAG setup, those candidates would be passed to the language model mostly as text. OpenDecoder keeps that text, but also attaches explicit quality indicators to the retrieved information. One indicator measures relevance: how strongly a retrieved piece appears to match the question. Another carries ranking information: where the retriever placed the document among the candidates, which acts as a rough sign of priority. A third is query performance prediction, which asks a broader question: for this query, does retrieval seem likely to have found good support at all? These signals become features available during decoding, the stage where the model repeatedly chooses the next piece of the answer. The output is still a generated answer, but the answer is produced with access to both document content and document-quality evidence. The abstract also says the approach is flexible enough to be integrated with post-training of language models and with different external evaluation information, so the mechanism is intended as a general way to let quality judgments shape generation rather than a single fixed scoring recipe.
29.math: The main mathematical idea is weighted evidence selection. Each retrieved document is a candidate source, but candidates do not all deserve the same influence. A relevance score turns a text-question match into a number so the system can compare documents. Ranking turns many candidates into an order, which matters because only a small set can fit into the answer process and higher positions usually receive more attention. Query performance prediction adds probability-style reasoning: it estimates, from signs around the query and retrieval results, how likely the retrieval step is to have produced useful evidence. These ideas fit the paper because the real decision is not whether to retrieve or not; retrieval has already happened. The decision is how strongly the generator should rely on each retrieved piece while forming the answer. The tradeoff is grounding versus distraction. More context can supply facts, but low-quality context can steer the model toward irrelevant or unsupported statements. By exposing quality scores to generation, OpenDecoder converts hidden retrieval uncertainty into visible control information. The numbers are not truth themselves. They are compressed judgments about usefulness, and compression can lose detail. But they give the model a structured way to treat a strong witness differently from a weak one.
29.dots: This paper sits squarely in the conference's retrieval-augmented generation family, where many papers ask how answer systems should govern outside evidence. It connects to ranking because the retrieved documents arrive in an order, and that order is a scarce-attention decision: which few pieces should be seen first by the answer writer. It connects to similarity because retrieval begins by measuring closeness between the question and documents, yet OpenDecoder recognizes that closeness alone does not guarantee usefulness. It also connects to probability through query performance prediction, which estimates uncertainty about the retrieval result itself. Neighboring RAG papers in the repo focus on conflict, graph structure, active retrieval, pruning, poisoning, or evidence chains. OpenDecoder addresses a complementary point in the same deeper problem: after retrieval has selected candidates, generation still needs explicit evidence-quality signals so noisy context does not receive the same treatment as direct support.
29.ww: The approach should help because it gives the generation stage information that a standard prompt may leave implicit or obscure. A language model can read fluent passages, but fluency is not the same as usefulness for the question. If one passage is highly relevant and another merely shares vocabulary, their raw text may not make that difference obvious enough during answer writing. Quality indicators act like margin notes on the evidence pile. They tell the model which passages the retrieval system ranked higher, which ones appear more relevant, and whether the query as a whole seems well served by retrieval. That extra channel is especially useful under noisy context, which the abstract names as the target condition. The mechanism does not need to perfectly identify the correct document every time. It only needs to reduce harmful equal treatment: strong evidence should have more influence, weak evidence should have less, and uncertain retrieval should be handled with more caution. That is a better fit than relying on the model to infer document quality only from text placement and wording.
29.po: The payoff is a RAG model that is better at using retrieved information when that information varies in quality. The abstract reports experiments on five benchmark datasets where OpenDecoder outperforms baseline methods and shows better behavior under noisy context. In practical terms, this buys an answer system that can still benefit from retrieval without assuming every fetched document is a good guide. The paper also claims flexibility: because the quality channel can incorporate relevance, ranking, QPP, and potentially other external evaluation information, the idea can be attached to different post-training purposes and retrieval setups.
29.limits: The method depends on the quality indicators being meaningful. If relevance scores, ranking scores, or query performance prediction scores are badly calibrated, stale, or biased toward surface matches, the generator may receive misleading confidence signals. The abstract does not show the full architecture details, the exact way the scores enter decoding, or whether the gains hold outside the five tested datasets. It also does not prove safety against poisoned documents or conflicts among sources; it addresses variable usefulness, not every trust failure in RAG. Finally, document quality is judged from available retrieval evidence, so the system still struggles if the collection lacks the needed answer or if all retrieved candidates are weak.
